html:
A rush for gold in the 1690s and 1700s in the hills of Minas Gerais ("general mines") in Portuguese Brazil. Bandeirantes, slave raiders and explorers from São Paulo, found the first rich deposits in the early 1690s. It became the longest gold rush in history and made Brazil the world's largest producer of gold in the 1700s.

Hundreds of thousands of people poured inland from the coast and from Portugal. Huge numbers of enslaved Africans were brought to work the rivers and mines. Towns such as Vila Rica, now Ouro Preto, grew rich and filled with baroque churches, the setting of the sculptor Aleijadinho. Diamonds were found too, in the 1720s.

The rush shifted Brazil's centre from the sugar coast of the northeast to the south. In 1763 the capital moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, the port for the mines. Much of the gold flowed to Portugal and from there to Britain, paying for British goods. By the late 1700s the deposits were running out.
